newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl goes on attack against opposition SPD.
newsitem.headline: Kohl goes on attack against opposition SPD.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Sunday broke Germany's traditional summer holiday lull and signalled the start of his 1998 re-election campaign with a sharp attack on his main rivals, the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

Kohl, going beyond the usual sedate style of Bonn political debate, accused the SPD not only of sabotaging a vital tax reform but of cynical exploitation of Germany's current problems, particularly its high unemployment.
"For party political reasons, the SPD does not want to help the economy and create jobs now," he said in a rare extended interview with the Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
"It wants to make sure we in the coalition get the blame for that now and that they profit in the 1998 elections," he continued.
He added that voters would nonetheless have the intelligence to see through this "transparent game" and vote him back in for a record fifth full term.

While Kohl has styled the tax reform a key weapon in the fight to cut Germany's 4.4 million jobless, the Social Democrats contend the package favours wealthy taxpayers and business at the expense of the poorest in society.

Kohl's attack on the SPD, which current opinion polls suggest could come to power next year in a "red-green" coalition with the Green party, comes amid an unusual degree of midsummer political activity.

Usually, Kohl's ritual summer trip to Austria's Wolfgangsee region is the opportunity for little more than carefully-posed shots of the chancellor taking his rest, admiring lakeside scenery or making forays into local shops.

But this year Kohl has already had to interrupt his holiday once to visit flood-stricken east Germany, trying to convince villagers there that all was being done to protect their homes from surging water levels.
His holiday calm was further broken by news from Bonn last week that his party negotiators had failed to persuade the SPD to give its blessing to the 30-billion-mark tax reform.

Knowing the Social Democrats' control of the upper house of parliament means they would block the tax bill if it came to a vote, Kohl must on Tuesday leave his holiday home again to attend a special parliamentary sitting on the matter.
Kohl's coalition is still wrangling over his cherished project of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), with Eurosceptics continuing at the weekend to raise the prospect of a delay.
But if things look shaky for Kohl, the Social Democrats appear to be having problems making political capital from the situation.

SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine's visit to the flood region last week hardly failed to inspire residents there and was roundly denounced at the weekend as blatant electioneering by the mass circulation Bild am Sonntag newspaper.
There is also speculation that the government might yet succeed with its tax reform as the SPD decides that continued opposition to it becomes too politically risky.
